title: Trump promoted $99 digital cards with a 47-card dinner and suit offer
description_short: A 2023 Trump digital-card promotion linked $99 cards to a 47-card dinner and mugshot-suit offer.
description_medium: In a December 2023 promotion, Trump offered Mugshot Edition digital cards for $99 each. CNBC reported that a buyer purchasing 47 cards in one transaction—a $4,653 bundle—would receive a physical card containing fabric from the suit Trump wore for his mugshot and a dinner at Mar-a-Lago. This verifies the sale and promotional terms, not the claimed $30 million total, royalties or licensing income.
description_long: In December 2023, Donald Trump promoted a Mugshot Edition of digital trading cards sold through CollectTrumpCards.com for $99 each. CNBC reported that purchasers buying 47 cards in one transaction would receive a physical card containing a piece of the suit Trump wore for his Georgia mugshot and a dinner at Mar-a-Lago. The 47-card bundle totaled $4,653, and the offer’s terms did not specify a dinner date. Forbes separately reported that the release comprised 100,000 cards and described additional limited-edition physical-card incentives. The official card site confirms the $99 price and presents the products as digital collectibles. These sources support a specific account of the product and event incentive, but they do not substantiate the old title’s claim of more than $30 million across four collections or establish total sales, royalties or licensing income. Those financial claims require financial disclosures or reliable reporting that directly measures the collections’ receipts. The revised title and descriptions therefore report the offer without converting a promotional price or purchase threshold into a revenue estimate.

title: CBO projected H.R. 1 Medicaid provisions would add 7.8 million uninsured by 2034
description_short: CBO estimated the House H.R. 1 Medicaid provisions would increase the uninsured population by 7.8 million by 2034.
description_medium: A June 2025 Congressional Budget Office analysis of Medicaid provisions in House-passed H.R. 1 estimated that they would increase the number of people without health insurance by about 7.8 million in 2034 relative to current-law projections. This is a bill-specific estimate, not 13 million people losing Medicaid coverage under a March administration budget proposal. The estimate concerns projected insurance coverage, not a count of current enrollees.
description_long: On June 24, 2025, the Congressional Budget Office published an estimate of Medicaid-related provisions in Title IV of H.R. 1, as passed by the House on May 22. CBO projected that enacting those provisions would increase the number of people without health insurance by about 7.8 million in 2034 compared with its baseline under current law. This is an estimate of the uninsured population associated with the bill’s Medicaid provisions, not a count of 13 million people who would all leave Medicaid. The prior description attached a broader 13-million figure to a March 2025 administration budget proposal and combined it with work requirements, per-capita caps, hospital warnings and other claims that the linked CBO material did not establish together. The revised title names the analyzed bill, the program area, the projected outcome and the year. It does not claim the proposal was a March administration budget, state that the estimate has already occurred, or treat the projection as an observed enrollment change. CBO’s bill-specific analysis is the source for this narrower result.

preserved_fields.title: Budget Proposes Medicaid Cuts: 13 Million to Lose Coverage
preserved_fields.description_short: Budget Proposes Medicaid Cuts: 13 Million to Lose Coverage
preserved_fields.description_medium: In March 2025, the Trump administration's budget proposal included provisions that independent analyses projected would result in 13 million Americans losing Medicaid coverage. The cuts were achieved through work requirements, per capita caps on federal Medicaid spending, and elimination of certain expansion populations. Hospitals in rural areas warned the cuts would force closures. Medical associations, patient advocacy groups, and even some Republican senators in Medicaid-heavy states expressed opposition. The Congressional Budget Office estimated the proposals would reduce federal Medicaid spending by over $800 billion over a decade.

notes: Reason: The linked CBO estimate concerns H.R. 1, not the March 2025 proposal, and returned 403. The packet does not substantiate the 13-million figure or combine it with the stated work requirements, per-capita caps, and hospital effects. Proposed correction: identify the proposal and date, then use its matching CBO estimate and distinct policy mechanisms.
Evidence resolution (2026-10-03): Replaced the mismatched March-budget/13-million framing with CBO publication 61510, a June 24, 2025 estimate specific to H.R. 1’s Medicaid provisions.
proposed_correction: Replace the mixed and misattributed 13-million claim with CBO’s specific 7.8-million uninsured estimate for the House H.R. 1 Medicaid provisions.

title: Sean Spicer disputed reporting on Trump’s 2017 inauguration crowd
description_short: At his first briefing, Sean Spicer challenged coverage of Trump’s inauguration crowd and asserted it was the largest ever.
description_medium: At a January 21, 2017 White House briefing, Press Secretary Sean Spicer accused the media of false reporting about Trump’s inauguration crowd and claimed it was the largest audience ever. He cited Mall capacity and Metro ridership figures. NPR and PolitiFact noted that the ridership comparisons and crowd estimates did not support the largest-ever claim. The supplied New York Times link concerns this crowd dispute, not the title’s rally epithets.
description_long: On January 21, 2017, White House Press Secretary Sean Spicer used his first briefing to challenge news coverage of Donald Trump’s inauguration crowd. Spicer said the media had engaged in “deliberately false reporting,” asserted that the Mall was full and claimed the event had the largest audience ever. He cited an estimated 720,000 capacity across areas of the Mall and 420,000 Metro riders, comparing the latter with 317,000 for Barack Obama’s 2013 inauguration. NPR reported that the 420,000 figure applied only through part of the day and that total Metro use on inauguration day in 2009 and 2013 was higher. PolitiFact also concluded that available measurements did not support the largest-ever claim. The White House transcript records Spicer’s statements, while the linked New York Times article addresses the crowd-size dispute. These sources do not support the old title’s claims that Trump called journalists “scum” or “human garbage” at rallies, nor its claims about threats to journalists, CPJ warnings or foreign leaders. The revised account stays with the documented briefing and press dispute.

preserved_fields.title: Trump Calls Journalists 'Scum,' 'Human Garbage,' 'Enemy' at Rallies
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Calls Journalists 'Scum,' 'Human Garbage,' 'Enemy' at Rallies
preserved_fields.description_medium: Throughout his first term, Trump used campaign rallies to direct physical hatred at journalists, calling them 'scum,' 'human garbage,' 'the enemy,' and other dehumanizing epithets while crowds cheered and sometimes turned threateningly toward press pens. Numerous journalists reported being surrounded by hostile crowds, receiving death threats, and facing physical intimidation at Trump events. The Committee to Protect Journalists repeatedly issued statements warning that Trump's rhetoric was the most dangerous environment for American journalists since Watergate. Several foreign leaders cited Trump's rhetoric to justify their own crackdowns on domestic press.

The populated medium is preserved unchanged. title: Trump Tower received a 421-a tax abatement valued at $22.5 million
description_short: A New York Times investigation reported a $22.5 million 421-a benefit for Trump Tower after a state court ruling.
description_medium: A 2016 New York Times investigation reported that Trump sought a 10-year tax abatement under New York City’s 421-a program for Trump Tower. After the city denied the benefit, the New York Court of Appeals ruled that the city had improperly blocked it; the Finance Department valued the abatement at $22.5 million. The report does not identify an affordable-unit requirement for this project or establish misuse.
description_long: A September 2016 New York Times investigation, republished by the Las Vegas Sun, examined public subsidies for Donald Trump’s New York real-estate projects. It reported that Trump sought a 10-year property-tax abatement under New York City’s 421-a program for Trump Tower, a luxury residential and commercial building. The city initially rejected the application, but the New York Court of Appeals later ruled that the city had improperly erected a barrier to the program’s benefit. The city Finance Department valued the 421-a benefit for Trump Tower at $22.5 million. The article separately reports a later $15 million tax break under another program for renovations to the tower’s commercial space; that amount is not part of the 421-a figure. The program was created to stimulate housing construction, but the supplied reporting does not identify an affordable-unit commitment attached to this particular abatement or establish that Trump violated the program. The revised title and description focus on the documented tax benefit and court history, avoiding an unsupported claim about affordable-housing obligations or misuse.
notes: The supplied synopsis describes luxury projects and public tax benefits, but the linked New York Times article returned 403 in the earlier review. The packet does not identify the properties, amount of tax savings or the affordable-housing commitments attached to each benefit.

The linked New York Times page returned HTTP 403; the supplied URL identifies a September 18, 2016 real-estate tax-break investigation. The carried-forward synopsis says it concerned New York City’s 421-a abatement and Trump luxury condominium projects, but the article could not be checked in this pass. The record lacks project names, abatement amounts, unit-level affordability commitments and evidence of compliance or misuse. Those project and tax records remain necessary to explain how the benefit applied.

Evidence resolution (2026-10-03): The original NYT article was readable through its Las Vegas Sun syndication. It identifies Trump Tower, the 421-a program, the Court of Appeals ruling and the $22.5 million value; it does not establish a project-level affordable-housing commitment or violation.

title: DHS announced a planned January 2020 end to Honduras TPS
description_short: DHS’s 2018 notice set a January 5, 2020 effective date for terminating Honduras’s TPS designation.
description_medium: In May 2018, the Department of Homeland Security announced it would terminate Honduras’s Temporary Protected Status designation, setting January 5, 2020 as the effective date and allowing an 18-month transition. The Federal Register notice provided a 60-day re-registration period from June 5 through August 6, 2018. This describes the announced schedule; it does not resolve later litigation or establish the ultimate status timeline.
description_long: On May 4, 2018, Homeland Security Secretary Kirstjen Nielsen announced that the Trump administration would end Honduras’s Temporary Protected Status designation. The Federal Register notice published on June 5 set the termination for 11:59 p.m. local time on January 5, 2020, eighteen months after the then-current designation was set to expire. It allowed Honduran beneficiaries to re-register from June 5 through August 6, 2018, with employment authorization extending to the planned end date. The notice said DHS had determined that conditions in Honduras no longer supported the designation. Associated Press reporting at the time estimated that about 57,000 Hondurans were affected. These sources support a description of the administration’s announced decision, its planned effective date and the re-registration period. The title should not state that TPS actually ended on that date without accounting for later litigation and agency actions. The linked DHS announcement and general AP topic page alone did not supply that later procedural history, so this description limits itself to the 2018 notice and its stated schedule.

title: Trump pardoned former Prince George’s County officer Stephanie Mohr in 2020
description_short: Trump granted Stephanie Mohr a full pardon on December 23, 2020, after she served 10 years for a civil-rights conviction.
description_medium: The Justice Department lists Stephanie Christine Mohr among Trump’s pardon recipients on December 23, 2020, for a District of Maryland conviction for deprivation of rights under color of law. A contemporaneous White House statement says she had served 10 years for releasing her police dog on a burglary suspect in 1995, causing a bite wound requiring ten stitches. The statement cites her service and time served as reasons for clemency.
description_long: On December 23, 2020, President Donald Trump granted a full pardon to Stephanie Mohr, a former Prince George’s County, Maryland, police officer and canine handler. The Justice Department’s pardon list identifies her federal conviction as deprivation of rights under color of law and records a 120-month prison sentence followed by two years of supervised release. A contemporaneous White House statement says Mohr released her police dog on a burglary suspect in 1995, causing a bite wound that required ten stitches, and says she served 10 years in prison. The statement describes support from the Law Enforcement Legal Defense Fund and the Fraternal Order of Police and presents her public service and lengthy prison term as reasons supporting clemency. These facts support a focused account of the pardon, underlying offense label, sentence and the administration’s stated rationale. The original DOJ index alone did not explain her conduct or the reason for clemency; the archived White House statement supplies that context. The statement is the administration’s account and does not replace the court record or establish Trump’s personal reasoning beyond the official explanation it gives.

The DOJ Office of the Pardon Attorney’s “Pardons Granted by President Donald J. Trump (2017–2021)” page (published 2017-08-28; modified 2024-10-23) was accessible. Its December 23, 2020 section lists Stephanie Christine Mohr, District of Maryland, with a 120-month prison sentence and two years’ supervised release (December 11, 2001) for deprivation of rights under color of law. The entry links an official clemency-record PDF, which returned a 277,964-byte PDF but could not be text-extracted with available tools. The index confirms the grant and prior sentence/offense, but gives no description of the conduct or reason for clemency. A case account establishing Mohr’s role and a sourced explanation for the pardon remain missing.

Evidence resolution (2026-10-03): The DOJ pardon index confirms Mohr’s grant, offense and sentence. The archived White House press statement supplies the underlying incident description and the administration’s stated rationale.
